pl-l3d6c2-d1e117.summary: Sets out the first opinion: in the incarnation a certain man was constituted of rational soul and human flesh, of which every true man consists; that man began to be God, not by God's nature but by the Word's person, and God began to be that man. They grant that man was assumed by and united to the Word and yet is the Word. 'God was made man' means God began to be a substance subsisting of soul and flesh, and that substance began to be God, not by migration of nature but with each nature's properties preserved. So it is truly said that God was made man and man God. They do not admit that this man is composed of the divine and human natures, but only of soul and flesh.
claims: God began to be a certain man subsisting of soul and flesh.
That man began to be God by the Word's person, not by nature.
The man is composed of soul and flesh, not of two natures.

pl-l3d6c2-d1e120.summary: Notes that they support their opinion with many testimonies, lest they seem to speak only from their own understanding.

pl-l3d6c2-d1e123.summary: Cites Augustine, De Trinitate: in 'the Word was made flesh' I understand by Word the true Son of God and by flesh the true son of man, and both together one person, God and man, joined by ineffable grace.
claims: Christ is one person, God and man, joined by grace.

pl-l3d6c2-d1e139.summary: Cites Augustine, Enchiridion: Christ is God from God and man born of the Spirit and Mary; both substances, divine and human, are the only Son of the Father; both are one, though one thing by reason of the Word and another by reason of the man; not two sons but one, God without beginning, man from a definite beginning.
claims: Both substances are the one Son of God.

pl-l3d6c2-d1e151.summary: Cites Augustine, Enchiridion again: what did human nature merit to be singularly assumed into the unity of the person of God's Son? No good will or works preceded; from the moment he began to be man he was nothing other than Son of God; as any man is one person of soul and flesh, so Christ is one person, Word and man.
claims: The assumed nature merited nothing prior to the union.
As soul and flesh make one man, so Word and man make one Christ.

pl-l3d6c2-d1e160.summary: Cites Augustine on John: we recognize twofold substance in Christ, divine, by which he is equal to the Father, and human, by which he is less; yet both together are one Christ, not two, lest God be a quaternity rather than a Trinity. So Christ is God, rational soul, and flesh.
claims: Christ is one, lest the Trinity become a quaternity.
Christ is God, rational soul, and flesh.

pl-l3d6c2-d1e169.summary: Cites Augustine, De praedestinatione sanctorum: how did that man merit to be assumed by the coeternal Word into unity of person and be the only Son of God? Nothing good of his preceded; by the Word making and assuming him, he began to be the only Son of God from the moment he began to be.
claims: The man assumed became Son of God by grace, without prior merit.

pl-l3d6c2-d1e178.summary: Adds from the same work: any man becomes a Christian by grace, just as by grace that man from his beginning became Christ.
claims: Christ's union is the exemplar of grace in Christians.

pl-l3d6c2-d1e184.summary: Cites Augustine, De Trinitate XIII: God's grace is commended to us in the man Christ, who did not attain by any prior merits to be joined to God so as to be one person with him as Son of God; from the moment he began to be man, he was also God.
claims: Christ was God from the moment he began to be man, without prior merit.

pl-l3d6c2-d1e194.summary: Cites Hilary, De Trinitate X: we do not doubt that Christ is God the Word, nor are we ignorant that the Son of Man consisted of soul and body.
claims: The Son of Man consisted of soul and body.

pl-l3d6c2-d1e206.summary: Sums up the first opinion: its holders, relying on these texts, say a certain man composed of rational soul and flesh was made God by grace, not nature; by grace alone, not merit or nature, that man had to be God and Son of God, with all the knowledge and power of the Word, with whom he is one person. The texts say not only that this man is one person with the Word and is the Word, but also that rational soul and flesh are the same person, Christ, and God.
claims: The man was made God by grace, not nature.
The assumed man has all the knowledge and power of the Word.

pl-l3d6c2.summary: Sets out the first opinion: in the incarnation a certain man was constituted from rational soul and human flesh, and that man began to be God, not by divine nature but by the person of the Word, and God began to be that man. Hence 'God was made man' means God began to be a certain substance subsisting of soul and flesh, and that substance began to be God, without change of nature; they do not say this man is composed of the two natures. They support this with Augustine (De Trinitate, Enchiridion, on John, De praedestinatione sanctorum) and Hilary: that man, with no prior merit, became the only Son of God by grace, so that Christ is God, rational soul, and flesh.
claims: First opinion: a man of soul and flesh began to be God by grace in the person of the Word.
On this view the man assumed is the Word, without change of nature.
That man became Son of God by grace, not by merit or nature.
